utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. Could the Registrar please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-03-69-PT, the Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Will both parties make their appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: On behalf of the Prosecutor, Dermot Groome, Camille Bibles, and Stephanie Wee as case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. For the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For Mr. Jovica Stanisic, Defence counsel Vladan Vukcevic and Mr. Knoops, who will introduce himself in a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vukcevic, and Mr. Knoops.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Mr. Knoops, appearing as co-counsel in the case of Mr. Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Knoops.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. I'm attorney Zoran Jovanovic and I am Defence counsel for the accused Franko Simatovic. Thank you

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. This is the first Status Conference according to Rule 65 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. And as the parties are aware, this conference is held in order to organise exchanges between the parties and to review the status of the case so as to ensure the expeditious preparation for trial. And first of all, I would note that the Chamber is now seized of the preliminary motions challenging the form of the indictment, filed by Defence counsels of both Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Simatovic, and also the Trial Chamber, as the Trial Chamber of Mr. Slobodan Milosevic, is seized of the motion asking for the access to the material of the Milosevic case. And the Chamber is deliberating on these issues and will file its decision in due course. Having said that, shall we move on to the issue of disclosure. And first, my understanding is that the Prosecution has completed its obligation under Rule 66(A)(i).

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I have this confirmed by the Defence counsels.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as the Defence counsel for Mr. Stanisic, I do confirm that we have received within the time period prescribed all the material relevant to the indictment, and we have lodged a complaint, and we expect your decision. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And how about for Mr. Simatovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the same goes for us. According to Rule 66(A), the material was disclosed in August, and we have filed a motion along those lines, as you yourself said, so that we have completed that part of the process. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Then if Mr. Groome could tell me the situation in relation to Rule 66(A)(ii) materials.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are in the process of finalising the witness list and with a view towards making the case as compact as possible, also selecting witnesses wherever possible that have testified previously so that we may apply to have their testimony heard via 92 bis. Recognising that the Court will set the schedule for the completion of that process, it is an ongoing process for us, and what the Prosecution would request, we would request a date in January, prior to the next Status Conference, for which we would have completed that process, as well as have filed a pre-trial brief and have met all of our obligations under 65 ter. I believe that would be the time that we would be able to reasonably comply with all the pre-trial obligations that the Prosecutor has.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I would very much encourage to stand by what you just now said. Is there anything to add for the Defence, to this comment by Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your permission, I'd like to say the following: On the 19th of September, that is to say, immediately prior to this Status Conference, we did receive this document from the Prosecution, in which we were informed of the tempo and manner in which the Prosecution would give us access to exculpatory and other material that they might have. In this brief we were also told that some electronic system was being prepared which would enable us to have speedier access into these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you, but we'll come to the Rule 68 in a minute. So if you have anything to add to the issue of disclosure of Rule 66(A)(ii).

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I didn't understand. I do apologise. I'll take the floor later on, then, thank you, when the time comes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. You don't have to apologise. Nothing from the -- from Mr. Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we are expecting disclosure on the part of the Prosecution, the sooner the better, of course. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Then, Mr. Groome, could you start on the exculpatory -- disclosure of exculpatory materials.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. But before I do that, if I might just -- one other disclosure provision in Rule 66. The Defence of Mr. Stanisic has invoked reciprocal discovery under 66(B). I'd ask them to confirm that on the record. And we will await some indication from them of what issues they feel are material to the Defence, and we will then search our files and make available to them as soon as practicable any disclosure that would be warranted under 66(B). I have no such indication from the Defence of Mr. Simatovic. I'm not sure if they are prepared to indicate one way or the other whether they seek disclosure under 66(B), but perhaps we could include the matters under Rule 66, and then I will discuss Rule 68.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Vukcevic, do you have anything to add to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, not at this point. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then let's move on to Rule 68.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect to Rule 68, a large portion of OTP's evidentiary collections will become available on line for the Defence counsel to search for evidence they believe is relevant to their case. The Prosecution requests that given the imminent availability that we not be required to search, print, and deliver the accused's documents from those searchable collections at this point, assuming that the implementation of that system goes as planned. With respect to the remaining collections and all other documents in evidence in the possession of the Prosecutor, we will be conducting searches of that material and provide it as it is identified. The method with which we will identify this material is by conducting electronic searches of keywords or phrases, and then reviewing all of the documents that contain those keywords or phrases, and then, in turn, disclosing any of those documents which contain Rule 68 material. Could I suggest that the Defence counsel provide to the Office of the Prosecutor, in writing, any keywords or search terms they believe will identify exculpatory material, and I will, in consultation with the people responsible for those computer searches, ensure the effective searching of those terms. We have, prior to this date, disclosed to Defence counsel a copy of the search terms presently used for Rule 68 searches in the Milosevic case on the belief that since many of the factual issues are overlapping, that may assist them. So if they can indicate to us in writing whether they a adopt those searches and whether they want any additional searches, we will begin the process of identifying that material and disclosing it. And then finally, Your Honour, outside of those two areas or sources of Rule 68 material we will, of course, continue to observe our obligation to disclose any material which we become aware of, that is, falls under Rule 68.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. As you mentioned just now, the Rule 68 obligation is an ongoing duty on the part of the Prosecution. So I'd like to remind that now. Yes, any comment from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you have just said what I was going to say as Defence counsel; that is to say, that Rule 68 does exist and the Defence calls for it to be complied with. Of course, with the introduction of an electronic system, things are made more easier, then we accept it. But we also take into consideration the preparation of our clients in their defence case, and electronic methods are completely impossible for them, in amassing exculpatory material. So we insist upon the application of Rule 68 as it has been stipulated in the documents. Thank you. Just that, for the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honour, any technical advancement in the sense of searching for material under Rule 68 is very welcome. However, the Rule as it stands now imposes upon the Prosecution the duties as -- concerned in Rule 68(A)(ii). So it is an ongoing, continuous duty of the Prosecution, which must take place without the active participation of the Defence. Of course, the Defence will not be passive, so if the Defence has any knowledge of any material being in the Prosecution's hands that could be considered to be exculpatory, it will take the initiative and have that material surface. However, this mustn't diminish the responsibility on the part of the Prosecution to disclose material pursuant to that Rule in a continuous fashion. And it is along those lines that I propose, or rather, I should like to stress that we do expect the Prosecution to function in the same way and the same tempo and speed in disclosing supporting material, material from other cases, where investigation has taken place. So we should like them to proceed in the same manner with respect to the exculpatory material. Now, disclosure up until January, as they have said, and the pre-trial brief as well, means that we're going to have a speedy process, in view of the indictment. Now, I'm afraid that we would be a bit late with the Rule -- material under Rule 68 if we expect the Defence to locate and stipulate what it wishes to obtain. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Rule 68 says that "The Prosecutor shall, as soon as practicable, disclose to the defence the existence of material known to the Prosecutor which in any way tends to suggest the innocence or mitigate the guilt of the accused," and so on. So that does not mean that the Prosecution should be necessarily proactive to find out all these mitigating materials. So in a practical sense, the cooperation from the Defence is necessary and requisite. So whether I can ask the Defence whether they are willing to cooperate in providing these search criteria, which can be used in electronic file search. Or is the Prosecution's offering that they come to the office and they can use the search engine themselves?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: There are actually two ways, Your Honour, and Your Honour is correct in both. The first body of material is material basically giving the Defence in this case the same access that our staff would have. We can, of course, if the Court so orders, we can search that, but I think the plan that has been worked on by the Registrar is that the Defence would be able to sit down and put in their own search criteria and identify any documents and then simply print them off. That is the majority of the evidentiary collection that is now in the possession of the Prosecutor's -- in the Prosecution's office. The second body of material, which includes statements and evidence provided to the Prosecutor under Rule 70, that will not be part of the system. And what I'm indicating is that we will undertake immediate searches of that material for Rule 68 material, using the search criteria that we've used in the Milosevic case, and I'm inviting my colleagues to submit additional search criteria that they would like us to search that body of material that will not be part of what I believe is called a disclosure suite. So I'm proposing that we begin with the material that they will not have access to. If it comes to pass that the disclosure suite is not satisfactory, we will of course then meet our obligation in other ways by proposing that we begin with the closed body material and begin searching that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As I said earlier, that I have to emphasise this thing once again, the cooperation. It's necessary. But the failure to cooperate does not necessarily mean that Prosecution is relieved from their Rule 68 obligation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I recognise that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And then having said that, can I recommend the parties, while you are here, to meet with the Prosecution after this meeting or conference, or tomorrow, to discuss those things, those practical matters in relation to Rule 68 materials. I note nodding. Can I take it as a positive answer? Thank you. And then did we hear about the reciprocal disclosure from the Defence? Just confirming what the Prosecution has said.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Not from the Defence. From Mr. Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Simatovic. Yes. Do you have any say on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At this point in time, the Defence of the accused Mr. Franko Simatovic is not in a position to disclose material to the Prosecution of this kind, but we will do so in due course on time. However, we cannot do so right now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I understand. I understand that there will be five expert witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this stage, that's not a firm number. It's an estimate of expert witnesses, and some of them will have testified in prior trials. So we may be seeking to introduce their report and their expert testimony under 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It may be too early to ask, but when do you think you can complete their disclosure, roughly?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: For some of them, Your Honour, I would think sometime in December or early January, and for the remainder, I think at that stage I will be able to identify for the Court a precise date if any additional or new experts are required, I would be able to identify a precise time schedule when we would expect those new experts to have their discovery completed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. It is my understanding that the Prosecution's office sent some list of sample facts to produce agreed facts in the later stage. Could you explain that to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would first recognise that we have met with Defence counsel just before this hearing and have, on a previous occasion, met with Mr. Jovanovic and Mr. Knoops. So in the spirit of cooperation, the Prosecutor has forwarded to the Defence, both Mr. Simatovic and Mr. Stanisic, some potential agreed facts. It is a very early list of facts at this stage, but it is a basis upon which to begin a discussion about which facts really aren't in dispute and which facts are. I would expect that list to change dramatically over the course of continuing negotiations and would expect by the time of the filing of the pre-trial brief that there would be a clear indication about what facts are agreed to and what facts are not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So it is based on the voluntary cooperation on the part of the Defence. They are not duty-bound to answer those questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I recognise that, Your Honour. This is simply a vehicle to begin negotiations about what facts are truly in dispute in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I'd like to hear some observation on this from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is premature to speak about the facts that have been agreed upon, the agreed facts, but I do recognise the efforts made by the Prosecution to indicate the agreed facts. As Defence counsel for Mr. Stanisic, I could agree that some of them are historical, geographical facts which are not in dispute, of course, but for the moment I don't see any link with the trial against Mr. Stanisic in view of the indictment issued. So it is too early for us to speak about these general facts which would not be in dispute. But once you have given me the floor, and I thank you for doing that, may I just make a remark and go back to a subject we broached earlier on? And it would mean a great deal to the Defence. At a meeting, pursuant to 65(E) and ter -- 65 ter that we had a month ago, the Defence counsels for Mr. Stanisic made a request, and we would like to reiterate it on this occasion. From the ruling on confirming the indictment as it stands, we can see that the distinguished Judge who got the indictment to confirm it on the 24th of April this year made certain remarks with respect to the indictment and later on these remarks were acted upon. We received a second indictment, which was then confirmed as well, on the 1st of May. And I don't think I need tell you that it is in the interests of the Defence to have the text of that first indictment that was confirmed, and especially the remarks that Judge Agius made on the occasion with respect to that first indictment. Because if the ruling of the Court is in place, then of course we would like to learn about it, and we would be very much interested in learning of that matter and the two indictments. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It has nothing to do with the Rule 66 or such disclosure. So having heard that, if Mr. Groome can give any observations.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, just before this hearing, Mr. Jovanovic once again requested that material. I must confess I'm not fully apprised of the jurisprudence regarding this. I told him that I would reconsider the matter and study the jurisprudence and would act accordingly after that. So I will -- there doesn't seem to be any formal motion before the Chamber at this stage for it. I will discuss my decision with Mr. Jovanovic informally, and if he seeks to formally apply for that, then I will respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I would -- yes, Mr. Simatovic. I beg your pardon. Mr. Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Just a slight digression. The request made by Mr. Vukcevic was made, and I would like to join in in asking for that too, if he does get what he has Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. requested. Now, the topic we broached before what my learned colleague Mr. Vukcevic just said with respect to accepting -- or rather, the agreed facts, there are 680 of them, in fact, if I remember correctly, these -- the facts stipulated. But as I say in my letter, I'm not quite clear on the status of this list of agreed facts, because it was stated that this could be an example, along with the letter attached to it by the Prosecution, attached to the list, that they might be facts which have nothing to do with this trial, in fact. But that, on the other hand, it could represent a basis for discussion. So I'd just like the Prosecutor to tell us, quite precisely: Are they facts offered to the Defence in this case, agreed facts? And is that what we're going to start off with? Or is it just something that is to be discussed and harmonised in due course with another list to be compiled? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My understanding is they are nothing but a sample, and if Defence seems to be cooperative, the OTP will be ready to send the list of facts in due course. Am I right in guessing so?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And I would also point out that we view this as a cooperative process. If there are facts that the Defence feels may not be in dispute, we would welcome their suggestion about those facts. And it may very well be that the Prosecution would then agree to those facts. So what was provided, as you say, was simply a sample to begin the process of discussing what facts are agreed to and what are not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Speaking for myself, it is also a good way for the Defence to send the list of facts which they think they shouldn't be in dispute at all. And coming to the disclosure of a previous indictment, my recommendation would be this: First wait for the Prosecution's reaction, whether they can give you or not; and if you can get it, and you feel like having it in the near future, my recommendation is to file it in official motion; and then it will be for the Chamber to deliberate on that, and the Chamber will give a ruling on that. And I think it's too early to discuss at this stage, for example, number of witnesses or length of trial, so let's have a discussion on the next Status Conference on those issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I would be able to provide precise numbers at that stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then is there anything to add for the parties? Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Not from the Prosecution, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that this is the right time to state the following: The Defence of Mr. Stanisic faces problems that are of an extra-legal nature. Namely, the condition of the health of Mr. Stanisic. This compels us to act in certain ways, and it is in this respect that we expect your assistance. Could you kindly give the floor to my colleague, Mr. Knoops, and he would be in a position to inform you about the plans of the Defence in this respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Knoops.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. First one to Rule 67(D), the Defence finds it appropriate to notify your Court and the Prosecution of the existence of additional evidence or material, the disclosure of which may be deemed in the interests of the case. This material relates to new and fairly important medical evidence about the accused. In light of this observation, the Defence wishes to inform your Court, as well as the Prosecution, of its intention to file a Rule 74 bis motion in order to have the accused's mental condition examined, and submit this new medical evidence. Secondly, the Defence herewith informs your Court and Prosecution of its intention to file in due course a motion for provisional release, which may be intertwined with the present medical condition of the accused. Although this Status Conference is probably not meant for elaborating in detail on the contents of these two motions, the Defence holds the opinion that it is in the interest of an efficient procedure to disclose their purpose so your Court and the Prosecution are able to anticipate these motions. In addition to the medical file which is already part of the material disclosed by the Prosecution, the Defence was provided last week with additional medical reports which can either be disclosed at this instance or together with the request for a Rule 74 bis motion, which will be filed according to schedule this week by the Defence. In this context, the following reports are disclosed. It pertains to ten reports from the period of 2001 to 2003, all being written by medical experts from Belgrade. The thing is, Your Honour, that the physical condition of the accused is deteriorating further and has severe potential effect on the mental condition. These reports also illuminate the causal relationship between the disease, on the one hand, and the mental condition of the accused, on the other hand. From this point of view, the proposed medical examination of Mr. Stanisic, through a forensic psychiatrist, seems quite relevant. Moreover, as mentioned in my letter to the case manager of your Court of the 22nd September, under paragraph 2, it is material to the Defence, and probably also to the other parties, to assess whether the accused is considered fit to stand trial, considering also the announcement of the Prosecution to disclose a significant part of the volume of potentially exculpatory evidence and material of the Milosevic case, amounting to almost 90.000 pages and 150 videotapes. Therefore, two questions emerge. A: Does there exist a relevant causal relationship between the disease of the accused and his mental condition, and if so, to what extent? And secondly, can the accused be considered to be mentally fit to face the mentioned trial and subsequent mental pressure stemming from this trial. Therefore, with regard to the above-mentioned medical information, the new information, the Defence firstly announces its intention to file a request for the appointment of a forensic psychiatrist in order to answer these two questions. Eventually, through a Rule 74 bis motion. To that end, the Defence proposes to appoint Dr. Offermans, an experienced Dutch forensic psychiatrist who is also affiliated to the psychiatric observation clinic of the Dutch Ministry of Justice in Utrecht. This expert has an extensive experience with regard to mental examination of accuseds. Despite the fact that this expert is, according to our information, not yet mentioned in the list of the Registry, we prefer to have him appointed eventually in conjunction with a second expert of the Prosecution's office. And secondly, we like to stress that we intend to file in due course a motion for provisional release, which, as stated before, could be intertwined with the present medical situation of the accused, which is quite concerning. And I think this is important also for your Court to realise that the reports we have now access to indicate that the mental situation also of the accused is deteriorating due to his severe illness. Thank you for your time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Knoops. I don't think I followed you in full when you said the relation between the vast scope of the 68 materials, for example, 90.000 materials, and health of the accused. Could you elaborate on that once again?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the only point the Defence wants to make is that it's not unlikely that we will face a long trial in this case, because also the materials which we added to the provisional and the supporting materials are considerable. And it's a question if the accused is properly fit to stand this lengthy trial. And therefore, the Defence seeks to have an examination, medical examination, for this purpose as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. You have the point. And correct me if I'm wrong. The Defence is going to file its Rule 74(D) motion in relation to provisional release motion, irrespective of provisional release.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Yes, irrespective, Your Honour. Yes. So the first intention of the Defence is to file 74 bis motion, and depending also on the outcome of that motion, we will consider the filing of a motion for provisional release. So first of all we think it's important to have this motion filed for a 74 bis ruling, to have the accused medically examined by a forensic psychiatrist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But on the part of Defence, you have already some expert opinions as to the health of the accused?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Yes, we have, Your Honour. We have in this -- at this moment, we have ten additional medical reports, based on the physical condition of the accused, but was not yet conducted a forensic examination of the accused. And the present reports indicate the existence of a causal relationship between the physical condition of the accused, on the one hand, and his mental condition. But again, for this specific issue, we think it would be appropriate to appoint an expert witness to conduct an examination specifically for that element, that medical element.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So what you are saying is that whether the Defence will file its provisional release motion will depend upon the outcome of the expert opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then I'll pass on this information to the Chamber. But you have to file the motion to get a ruling on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Of course. That's clear, Your Honour. We intend to file the 74 bis motion already this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Just to say, from the Prosecution's point of view, we would of course not oppose any examination, medical, of Mr. Stanisic. I do have some concerns that the expert selected does not speak Mr. Stanisic's language, and we would be seeking to file a similar motion to have a Serbo-Croatian-speaking psychiatrist conduct an examination, as we believe that would be more appropriate to have that -- an expert, we actually have somebody in mind. So just to let the Chamber know that it may anticipate a similar motion from the Prosecution of this nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll see. And is there any matters to raise at this moment, or from the accused? Yes, Mr. Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I would just like to raise one more question, but could we please move into private session in order for me to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is that what you were going to say? Yes. I have in mind to have a next Status Conference around 20th January next year, just before the deadline for the next Status Conference. And unless there's anything to be raised, the hearing is adjourned.
